items.label: 9A
items.fix: Show quantities that never vary among the simulated copies (Data centers' overdue orders, phantom orders and lead time) as fixed by the model's structure instead of with a spread ratio of 1.00. When a quantity has no spread with or without data, the measure falls back to exactly 1. That reads as "comes from assumptions" when the quantity is simply constant for this kind of business.
items.test: Rebuild the Evaluation pages for this world; Data centers' overdue orders, phantom orders and lead time should show as fixed by structure rather than 1.00.

items.label: 7A
items.fix: When checking sector totals against official statistics, include the statistic's own uncertainty, the amount the filter already assumes when it pulls totals toward it. Today the range is only the spread between the model's copies and the statistic's draws. Because the filter pulls each copy toward its own draw, that spread is very small, and gaps under 1% count as misses.
items.test: Rebuild the Evaluation pages for this world; Hotels and Hospitals employees and Chemicals and Food utilization should move toward 90/100, while Machinery production (5.8% off) should still disagree.

items.label: 5B
items.fix: Widen the forecast range for capacity on its own, with a factor set so that the range holds the next run's estimate about 90% of the time on earlier synthetic worlds. Today one widening factor serves every quantity, and capacity, which the data pin down well at each run, ends up too narrow for how much the level moves between runs.
items.test: Refilter existing runs of earlier worlds to set the factor, then rescore this world; Capacity's hit rate on Forecasts against later estimates should be near 90/100.

items.label: 6A
items.fix: Replace the single widening factor for all ranges with one factor per quantity and forecast horizon, set on several earlier synthetic worlds where the truth is known. Today every quantity is widened by the same amount (about 1.9 times for forecasts), set on an older world before several model changes. Quantities the data pin down need less widening than quantities that come mostly from the model.
items.test: Refilter and rescore existing runs of earlier worlds to set the factors, then rescore this world; on Forecasts against later estimates most quantities should land between 85/100 and 95/100 instead of 74-100/100.

items.label: 8A
items.fix: Add observations of input inventory, such as official materials inventories for manufacturers and companies' reported raw materials. No observation measures input inventory today, which is why its spread ratio is near 1 in all eight sectors that have it. Without data, nothing else in the model can pin it.
items.test: Rebuild the world with these observations and run a full four-date backtest; input inventory's spread ratios on What the data pin down should drop below 0.8.

items.label: 3B
items.fix: Add official statistics that measure new orders directly: manufacturers' new orders for Machinery and Semiconductors, new home sales for Housing, and newly signed leases for Data centers. Today no observation measures new orders, so they are inferred from the order book and shipments. Measuring them directly would pin them.
items.test: Rebuild the world with the new statistics and run a full four-date backtest; new-orders spread ratios on What the data pin down should drop below 0.8 in those sectors.

items.label: 6B
items.fix: Mark quantities whose spread ratio is 0.8 or above on Forecasts against later estimates, and leave them out of the overall hit rate. For these the later estimate also comes from the model's equations, so the check compares the model with itself, which is why input inventory and lead time score 100/100. The overall figure would then describe only quantities the data inform.
items.test: Rebuild the Evaluation pages for this world; the overall hit rate should describe only data-informed quantities, and the 100/100 rows should be marked as checked against the model itself.

items.label: 10B
items.fix: Measure how much each parameter is learned by comparing its uncertainty after fitting with its uncertainty given only the group's average, not the starting guess. Today the pull toward the group average counts as learning, so the 91% figure can flatter weakly observed entities. The figure will probably fall, but it will then show where the data truly shape the estimates.
items.test: Rebuild the Evaluation pages for this world; What the data pin down should report both the current and the stricter figure for every sector.

items.label: 3A
items.fix: Let the filter adjust each entity's order level in the sectors where new orders become less certain with data (Housing, Retail, Data centers, Machinery, Airlines), as it already does in Semiconductors. Today the order level is a fixed parameter, so observations of the order book, shipments and occupancy can only move orders through monthly surprises, which push the copies apart. With the level adjustable, the same observations can narrow it.
items.test: Rerun those five sectors at four run dates on two seeds; their new-orders spread ratios on What the data pin down should fall below 1.

items.label: 5A
items.fix: Add a small monthly capacity revision to every kind of business, as pipeline producers already have, so that capacity can drift away from its planned path. In forecasts the copies would then spread out further ahead, and stated-capacity observations could correct the level. Today capacity can change only through its fitted growth rate, so the range stays as narrow as today's well-known level.
items.test: Run a full four-date backtest; Capacity on Forecasts against later estimates should move from 74/100 toward 90/100 without a larger gap.

items.label: 10A
items.fix: Move the parameters that data rarely pin for each entity (emissions slope, capacity growth, list-price gap) to one value per sector, chosen sector by sector by how well each choice predicts withheld observations. Past tests found that sharing parameters helped Food, helped Machinery only when the starting guess was close, and hurt Steel. The choice has to be made per sector, not everywhere.
items.test: Run withheld-observation checks at two run dates in the sectors with the weakest parameters, then a four-date run with the chosen settings; the share of parameters learned from data should rise without worse forecast gaps.

items.label: 1A
items.fix: Give Wholesale an official price statistic, such as a monthly price index for wholesale trade. Wholesale has no price observations and no official statistic, and on an earlier synthetic world its price and unit cost drifted 10-12% off by the later run dates, which a later re-estimate then corrects. Pinning the price level would also pin the volume that the revenue observations imply.
items.test: Rebuild the world with the price statistic and rerun Wholesale at all four run dates on two seeds; Wholesale's gap on Forecasts against later estimates should fall well below 12.4% and its hit rate rise toward 90/100.

items.label: 9C
items.fix: Add observations of advance bookings: rooms and seats already booked for coming months for Hotels and Airlines, and leases signed but not yet started for Data centers, where that observation is still sparse. These measure the order book in service businesses directly.
items.test: Rebuild the world with booking observations and run a full four-date backtest; order book and lead time spread ratios in Hotels and Data centers should drop below 0.8.

items.label: 4A
items.fix: Compute the spread ratio from total spread over the history with and without data, rather than averaging month-by-month ratios, and report months where single copies ran away. Averaging lets a few months in which copies barely disagree without data produce very large values, so if that is the cause the ratios will shrink, and if not, the measure shows where the problem lies.
items.test: Refilter the existing fits at all four run dates with the new measure; Retail's ratios of 3.2-3.6 and the other values above 1.2 on What the data pin down should fall toward or below 1, or the runaway months should be identified.

items.label: 2A
items.fix: During fitting, anchor the overall size of Machinery's representative entities to the official production statistic, as 11 other sectors already do, since a steady 5.8% gap points to the size of the untracked firms. On an earlier world this hurt Machinery (error 5.6% to 7.9%), but that was before a fix to dollar-valued order-book observations, which matters because Machinery is measured in dollars.
items.test: Rerun Machinery at four run dates on two seeds with the anchor; on Sector totals against official statistics, Machinery production should move from 0/100 toward 90/100 with a gap under 2%.

items.label: 2B
items.fix: Let the filter adjust Machinery's order level and overdue orders directly, as it already does for Semiconductors, so the sector-wide unfilled-orders statistic can correct the order book month by month. In Semiconductors this ended runaway order books, and their results were mild in five of five backtests. Machinery shows the same signs: it misses too many observations and its new orders become less certain when data are added.
items.test: Rerun Machinery at four run dates on two seeds; Observations against the model should move from 85/100 toward 90/100, and the official production and utilization statistics should agree more often.

items.label: 9B
items.fix: Let the filter adjust the order level of Hotels, Hospitals and Data centers directly, so that occupancy, load-factor and staffed-bed observations can move demand rather than only output. Today a reading that shows a fuller hotel can change little in the order side. This is the same change that steadied Semiconductors' order book.
items.test: Rerun those three sectors at four run dates on two seeds; their shipments, order book and lead time spread ratios should fall below 0.8.

planned_by: the most likely fixes first, none less likely than Coin Flip, while the plan's expected cost stays at most $100; the tests run in parallel, each expected to take under 24 hours
